papers.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
papers.workshop_title: Do Robots Need World Models? A Debate on Dynamics Learning, Planning, and End-to-End Robot Learning
papers.summary: LeWAM jointly learns action-conditioned latent dynamics and a flow-matching action policy. It can sample actions directly or refine candidate plans by differentiating through the learned dynamics. Its goal-image planning experiments and goal-free behavior-cloning experiments test different uses of that model family. The physical-robot experiments use direct policy execution; they do not demonstrate that online planning improves every physical task. Models are trained or adapted for individual tasks and embodiments.

papers.title: Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination
papers.workshop_title: Do Robots Need World Models? A Debate on Dynamics Learning, Planning, and End-to-End Robot Learning
papers.summary: Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.

papers.title: Rolling-WAM: World Action Models with Rolling Imagination
papers.authors: Yinghua Zhou et al.
papers.workshop_title: Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI
papers.summary: Rolling-WAM distributes joint video-action denoising across successive control updates. It completes the next action chunk while retaining partially refined future chunks, then incorporates a new observation as the window advances. The paper evaluates simulation benchmarks and three Unitree G1 manipulation tasks. Its timing comparison measures steady-state replanning rather than startup or the complete robot lifecycle. The authors also identify a trade-off: retained future predictions can lag behind rapid scene changes, particularly with long windows.

papers.title: Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force
papers.authors: Jaden Clark, Changhao Wang, Yihuai Gao, Seongheon Hong, Hojung Choi, Mark Cutkosky, Yifan Hou, Shuran Song
papers.workshop_title: Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?
papers.summary: MuSe asks how a policy pretrained without a sensor can acquire that modality later while preserving its earlier capabilities. The studied case adds force-torque sensing to a pretrained Unified Video-Action model. Early token fusion and later cross-attention adapters combine the sensor with vision and other inputs; the model predicts future observations, force-torque signals and actions. During adaptation, replay mixes the original pretraining data with new multisensory demonstrations, masking the force input and force loss where those measurements are absent. The evaluation separates force prediction on previously unsupervised tasks, forward transfer to new contact-rich tasks and backward transfer to pretraining tasks. The authors report improvements in their tabletop settings, while no-replay ablations exhibit substantial forgetting. This is evidence for a particular sensor-expansion and replay strategy, not a result that every added sensor improves every policy. Only force-torque expansion, limited tasks and access to the original pretraining data were tested; broader modalities, embodiments and longer horizons remain future work.

papers.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
papers.authors: Maximilian Du, Zhanyi Sun, Chen Xu, Paarth Shah, Masha Itkina, Shuran Song
papers.workshop_title: Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?
papers.summary: Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. For diffusion policies, the project measures action disagreement through conditional denoising to reduce confusion from multiple valid action modes. Controlled experiments remove or enrich these anchors while keeping the replay budget comparable, and the authors report changes in forgetting in simulation and diagnostic real-robot task sequences. The project also emphasizes that replay cannot consist only of high-conflict anchors: diverse old experience remains important. This is persistent policy training from selected past data, not inference-time conversational memory. Extracting anchors needs the model’s representation space and past training data; the evaluated task sequences and robots do not establish unlimited continual deployment.

papers.title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
papers.workshop_title: Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?
papers.summary: RARA reuses selected pretraining demonstrations to guide task adaptation. It retrieves trajectories by instruction similarity, then matches target frames to relevant source phases by action-chunk similarity. First it trains representation-producing layers and a small projector to align target features with frozen pretrained features. It then behavior-clones the target task while constraining how the policy represents the retrieved source observations. Retrieved source actions form alignment pairs; they are not extra behavior-cloning targets. In the reported diffusion-policy and GR00T experiments, this combination improves adaptation under visual shifts. Data choice is crucial: using unrelated pretraining skills or random pairings can remove the gain and sometimes hurt performance. The method therefore supplies a selection-and-preservation perspective on post-training, rather than a claim that anchoring any prior representation is beneficial. The experiments keep the robot and action space fixed and require relevant pretraining data.

papers.title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs
papers.authors: Junhyeong Park, Wook Jung, Taeyoung Kim, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin
papers.workshop_title: Scaling H2R: Scaling Laws and Diversity in Human-to-Robot Workshop
papers.summary: This Scaling H2R workshop contribution adapts a robot-pretrained VLA with unpaired human and robot demonstrations. It tackles two interfaces separately. A hand-geometry training objective aligns the policy’s observation representation, while a shared action tokenizer uses independent human and robot reconstruction decoders instead of forcing both sources through one mapping. Human actions are reconstructed and retargeted to a canonical wrist–hand convention before tokenization. The tokenizer is frozen during policy adaptation, and the reported transfer uses a fixed human-trained decoder branch whose outputs already follow that control convention. Real-robot experiments cover object transfer and skills introduced through human demonstrations in a shared environment. The reported task scores include partial progress, so they must not be presented as binary success percentages. Each comparison condition uses one independently trained policy; the evidence is narrower than unrestricted cross-embodiment or in-the-wild generalization.

Across three models and two video benchmarks, we investigate whether similar responses emerge in vision-language-action models by examining their internal representations and action tendencies in response to visible hazards and harmful consequences. papers.title: EMBODIEDSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics
papers.authors: Yilang Liu, Zeyu Shen, Haoxiang You, Zhicheng Zheng, Lihan Zha, Kashu Yamazaki, Mingtong Zhang, Suning Huang, Jiankai Sun, Qianzhong Chen, Luxi He, Kaiyuan Liu, Haoran Chang, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Mac Schwager, Dhruv Shah, Peter Henderson, Ian Abraham, Canwen Xu
papers.workshop_title: Workshop on Agentic Robotics
papers.summary: EmbodiedSWE separates coding agents as task solvers from coding agents as sources of policy supervision. Its benchmark contains human-designed long-horizon, contact-rich simulation tasks. Agents inspect privileged simulator state and iteratively produce executable solution programs; an isolated grader checks submitted artifacts. Verified solutions then seed EmbodiedSWE-Gen, which diversifies scenes, strategies, intermediate phases and perturbations, retaining trajectories after grader and replay checks. Those demonstrations fine-tune VLAs, so the resulting neural policy update is distinct from the coding agent’s program search. The authors test data scaling and held-out variations, and show a real four-stage lamp-disassembly example trained only on generated simulation demonstrations. That physical result covers one task and ten trials, with limited full-task completion. Appendix I also distinguishes these component studies from a broader synthetic-task-generation-to-policy pipeline that has not been run end to end. A separate exploratory RL post-training experiment for the coding agent lacks held-out checkpoint evaluation. The work provides a useful teacher-data route, not proof that all coding-agent capability has already been distilled into a general robot.

papers.title: PhysCaP: Grounding Code-as-Policy Agent with Physics-Informed Exploration
papers.authors: Chen-Yu Lin, Jing-Wen Chen, Hsueh-En Chang, Hung-An Chen, Sheng-Hsun Chang, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Min-Hung Chen, Yi-Ting Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Shao-Hua Sun
papers.workshop_title: Workshop on Agentic Robotics
papers.summary: PhysCaP gives a code-as-policy agent explicit ways to acquire physical information that an image alone may not reveal. Training-free modules estimate object mass using differential joint torque during a lift and stiffness using gripper force-displacement measurements. A Planner decides what information is missing and when exploration can stop; a Prioritizer filters and orders candidate interactions; a coding agent produces programs that call measurement and control APIs. Measurements update a task belief before further exploration or execution. The evaluated improvement is therefore in information gathering and programmatic control, rather than a new neural policy trained online. The study reports three physical tabletop tasks and a simulated hidden-mass task, with component comparisons that distinguish having measurement tools from choosing efficient interactions. Interaction-count and execution-time statistics are conditional on successful episodes. Simulation exposes a mass-sensing API only after a verified lift. These conditions are important when interpreting comparisons with passive policies; the experiments do not establish that all VLAs lack active perception or that the agent can infer arbitrary physics.

papers.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
papers.authors: Runyu Lu, Yubo Wu, Ethan Kou, Haotian Lin, Letian Fu, Wenli Xiao, Ajay Mandlekar, Yinzhen Xu, Guanya Shi, Ken Goldberg, Ang Chen, Mosharaf Chowdhury, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Guanzhi Wang
papers.workshop_title: Workshop on Agentic Robotics
papers.summary: ASPIRE learns robot control programs and reusable repair knowledge while keeping its underlying LLM frozen. Its execution engine exposes per-primitive multimodal traces so an actor can locate failures in perception, planning, grasping or control. Evolutionary search explores several candidate programs using debug seeds. Validated repairs are proposed as compact skill guidance containing a failure signature, when-to-apply condition, repair strategy and sometimes a code sketch. A fresh verifier actor checks a proposed skill on its source task before admission, and later actors retrieve the library as context. The learned artifact is thus executable code and persistent repair guidance, not an online update to the LLM’s neural weights. Evaluation separates debug and held-out seeds, with distinct procedures for different benchmarks. Simulation-discovered skills help real-robot debugging, but the paper explicitly says transfer is not direct policy deployment. The real cube study still uses human task guidance, scrambling and scene resets. One-time skill admission also leaves stale or misleading entries as an unresolved scaling issue.

papers.title: RLE-Bench: A Qualifying Exam for Coding Agents as Robot Learning Engineers
papers.authors: Haitong Ma, Chenxiao Gao, Rushi Qiang, Bo Dai, Na Li
papers.workshop_title: Workshop on Agentic Robotics
papers.summary: RLE-Bench evaluates a coding agent’s robot-learning engineering process, not only the controller it finally produces. Nine tasks span interactive control, policy development, perception and estimation, and mechanical design. Depending on the task, the submitted artifact may be retained agent context, a harness for a fresh agent, an exported policy, a training recipe, an estimator or a mechanical design. The benchmark constrains development time, interactions and compute, then tests the result under hidden conditions. Its overview also distinguishes three interface levels: low-level APIs, reusable robotics tools, and privileged simulator state. These interfaces matter when interpreting agent comparisons. The public technical report includes cases in which visible objectives or development tests fail to predict broader checks, reinforcing the value of independently held-out evaluation. The benchmark does not establish field reliability for generalist robots: some transfer is explicitly sim-to-sim, aggregate charts were unreadable here, and reported API cost excludes simulation and GPU infrastructure.

coverage_notes: Counts describe workshop entries, including the same work appearing in multiple workshops; they are not counts of unique archival main-conference papers.

The 39 accepted Agentic Robotics workshop papers are established by that workshop’s primary list. Their count is not substituted for the separate 39 late-breaking results reported in the main-stage opening remarks.
A workshop list can establish acceptance and available metadata; it does not establish that the full paper or its experiments were reviewed.
OpenReview browser-verification and PDF-access errors prevented completion of lists that rely on that portal. Dynamic or missing title lists remain explicitly unresolved.
Some sources publish abbreviated authors or filenames only; those metadata limits are retained rather than filled from guesses.
Graph connections and topic tags are curator reading suggestions. They do not assert that papers cite one another or validate another paper’s results.
display_note: The library publishes short source excerpts and primary links. Full source text was read for catalogue acquisition; a brief does not imply a full manuscript review.
